title: Profile the Overnight Note
subtitle: Find the record hiding in the note
scenario: It is 6:05 AM at Meridian Energy, and the brief ships at 7:00 whether it is ready or not. Everything the workflow knows about the 2 AM ERCOT spike is one paragraph the Overnight Desk Analyst typed. Before anything can be automated, prove exactly what that paragraph is carrying.
input: Checked overnight prices. ERCOT hub spiked around 2am, hit $187/MWh briefly then settled near $142/MWh. Wind generation underperformed, about 60% of forecast. Gas prices up slightly. Trader flagged the hub spike for review. No action taken yet. Need approval if we move on this.
instructions: Read the note once as a person, then again as a designer: which spans carry field values?
Tag each of the five intake fields to the span that holds its value.
The leftovers are context, not data - that is the lesson.
Validate to mint the source profile.

segments.text: Wind generation underperformed, about 60% of forecast.
Trader flagged the hub spike for review. Need approval if we move on this.

fields.label: hub
fields.explain: The hub is the market this whole morning turns on. Only one span names a trading hub - and it is the one that spiked.

fields.label: peakPrice
fields.explain: The peak is what ERCOT hit briefly at 2 AM; the settle is where it ended. The brief cites both, so the record keeps them as two separate fields.

fields.label: settledPrice
fields.explain: Settled is the calmer price after the spike passed - not the brief peak, and not the time it happened.

fields.label: generationFlag
fields.explain: The operating story behind the spike: wind came in around 60% of forecast. That one span carries both the source and its performance - gas moving slightly is background, not the flag.

fields.label: approvalRequired
fields.explain: The control signal is the trader's ask: flagged for review plus need approval means approvalRequired is true. 'No action taken yet' describes the past, not the requirement.

intro.artifactPreviewNote: These are the five fields of the intake record you will build at 6:15. This lesson proves where each one lives in the source.
intro.heading: Before you tag: sources come first

sections.title: Why inspect before building
sections.body: Automation projects fail at the inputs more often than at the logic. Before extracting anything, a designer profiles the source: who produces it, in what shape, behind what access. Here: the Overnight Desk Analyst, prose, and a channel you would need permission to read.

sections.title: Prose is a format too
sections.body: This note is unstructured, but it is still a feed - it arrives every morning, from the same role, with roughly the same content. Recognizing prose as a recurring input is what makes it automatable at all.

sections.title: Lab vs work
sections.body: In the lab the note is a local text fixture. At work it would be an email, a Teams post, or a terminal note - and ingesting it would need channel access and permission. The workflow map records both realities.

sections.title: Why the JSON matters
sections.body: Downstream automation reads fields, not sentences. Until hub, peakPrice, and approvalRequired exist as named fields, the risk check and the approval route cannot see this morning at all. Tagging proves the fields exist before the intake step mints them.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: By hand you'd open the analyst's email, highlight the phrases that carry the hub, both prices, the wind status, and the approval ask, and key each one into a named column - so later steps read fields, not prose.

points: You tagged the five spans that become the intake record's fields: hub, peakPrice, settledPrice, generationFlag, approvalRequired.
Everything you did not tag is commentary - useful to a person, invisible to automation until someone maps it.
The lab's note is a local fixture; at work this same step is inbox or channel access plus the same field mapping.
The workflow can now identify where the morning market signal enters the system.
